title: Conversational implicature
text: Conversational implicatures are cases where what a hearer infers from an utterance goes beyond the literal sentence meaning and depends on conversational context.

title: Cooperative Principle
text: Grice proposed that conversational participants generally contribute what is required by the accepted purpose or direction of the conversation.

title: Maxim of Quantity
text: The Maxim of Quantity concerns providing as much information as is required for the current conversational purpose, while avoiding unnecessary additional information.

title: Maxim of Quality
text: The Maxim of Quality concerns making contributions that are true and avoiding claims for which the speaker lacks adequate evidence.

title: Maxim of Relation
text: The Maxim of Relation is commonly summarized as being relevant to the current purpose of the conversation. Apparent departures from relevance can contribute to conversational implicatures when context supports such an inference.

title: Maxim of Manner
text: The Maxim of Manner concerns clarity and orderly expression, including avoiding obscurity and ambiguity and striving for brevity and order.

title: Context dependence of implicature
text: A conversational implicature can depend on the conversational context. The same sentence can support different inferences when used in different conversational situations.

title: Cancelability of conversational implicature
text: Conversational implicatures are described as cancelable: a speaker can explicitly or contextually prevent an otherwise plausible implicature from arising.

title: Hedging as indirect language
text: Hedging can refer to language used to avoid giving a direct answer or opinion. Examples include expressions such as 'it could be' and 'seems'.

title: Premises and conclusions
text: An argument contains premises that provide support for a conclusion. The relationship between premises and conclusion can involve logical implication, probability, relevance, or other forms of support.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Argument and Argumentation

title: Logical consequence
text: A conclusion is a logical consequence of premises when the conclusion follows from those premises. In a valid deductive argument, if the premises are true, the conclusion must also be true.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Logical Consequence

title: Implicit or unstated premises
text: Informal logic can identify components of an argument that are not explicitly expressed. An implicit premise can be an unstated assumption that connects an expressed premise to a conclusion.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Informal Logic

title: Premise sufficiency
text: An argument can contain premises that are relevant to a conclusion without providing enough support for that conclusion. Informal logic distinguishes relevance from sufficiency of support.

title: Fallacious reasoning
text: A fallacious argument can appear legitimate while failing to provide adequate support for its conclusion. Studying fallacies includes examining whether premises are acceptable, relevant, and sufficient.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Argument and Argumentation

title: Irrelevant conclusion
text: An irrelevant-conclusion error occurs when an argument provides reasoning that does not actually address the claim at issue. The evidence may concern a different proposition from the conclusion being evaluated.

title: Appeal to authority
text: An appeal to authority can become fallacious when a claim is supported by an authority who is not actually an appropriate or relevant authority for the subject at issue.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Argument and Argumentation

title: Argumentation as communication
text: Argumentation is the communicative activity of producing and exchanging reasons to support claims or defend or challenge positions, especially where there is doubt or disagreement.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Argument and Argumentation

title: Inductive support
text: In inductive reasoning, premises can make a conclusion more likely without logically guaranteeing that the conclusion is true. The conclusion therefore goes beyond what is strictly contained in the premises.
source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Argument and Argumentation
